topics.topic: A NEW VOCABULARY LIST BUILT AROUND THE HIS/HER POSSESSIVE SUFFIXES - far and away the hour, and the first genuinely GRAMMATICAL block of the semester. She had already taught -ii (my) and -ka/-ki (your m/f); today she added -uhu (his) and -uhaa (her), both requiring a Damma on the last letter of the noun before the suffix, and she drilled them by round-the-room recall across every noun they own: ismuhu/ismuhaa (his/her name), kitaabuhu/kitaabuhaa (book), baabuhu/baabuhaa (door), baytuhu/baytuhaa (house), waajibuhu/waajibuhaa (homework), akhbaaruhu (his news), akhuuhu (his brother), ukhtuhu (his sister), Taalibuhaa (her male student), ustaadhuhu (his teacher). Her own warning on this: 'Those need a lot of practice, guys, because they're totally different from English' - she compared it to how hard the ENGLISH possessive was for her, 'why do I have to add 2 pronouns at the beginning, at the end.' The new words themselves: tafaDDal / tafaDDalii / tafaDDaluu (masculine / feminine / plural) - the all-purpose polite 'go ahead, come in, please take it', which is literally what she says when she calls someone to the board, so the gendered form is audible every class; Shami itfaDDal / itfaDDalii, which she noted carries a hamza at the beginning; yalla ('let's go', which she flagged as NOT respectful, against tafaDDal which is very respectful); SaaHib / SaaHibii / SaaHiba / SaaHibatii and rafiiq / rafiiqii / rafiiqatii (friend - see the register caveat in off_slide, which overrides the book); huwa / hiya (he / she, Shami huwwe / hiyye) with the rule that Arabic has NO NEUTRAL - every noun is masculine or feminine, 'even if you're referring to a dog or even if you're referring to a tree, a tree in Arabic is feminine'; amriikii / amriikiyya; Taalib / Taaliba (student - 'notice it's a capital T, so this is the harsh T', i.e. Taa' not taa'); ustaadh / ustaadha (which covers Mister, teacher AND professor - the borrowed profesor/profesora exists because Arabic has no P); jaami'a (university); and Saff (class), which she handed over mid-translation after discovering they had never been given it. She closed the block with five Arabic-to-English translation sentences and then set a pair/trio speaking task (introduce yourself and your partner, including where he is from - 'huwa min Virginia'), which ran out the recording

HAMZA, SECOND PASS - the board work included, and explicitly framed as one instalment of a staged plan rather than a finished topic: 'Hamza is so complicated in Arabic, so we're going to give it to you gradually... we'll talk little bit today and then we'll leave it until the end of the semester.' What she added on top of the 9/22 introduction: at the START of a word the only possible seat is alif, and the tashkiil on it decides the vowel (fatHa a, Damma u, kasra - which must be written UNDER the alif - i); an alif-hamza can carry sukuun but the sukuun is not written; hamza in the MIDDLE and at the END, where it may sit on alif, on waaw, or bare ON THE LINE, which is what she calls it ('this is Hamza on the line'). The payoff example for the on-the-line hamza is the NAME OF A LETTER THEY SAY EVERY DAY: the letter is baa', with a hamza and a sukuun, 'but out of laziness you say ba' - which is why she pronounces the letter names the way she does. New REQUIRED vocabulary came out of this: akh (brother, alif-hamza with fatHa) and ukht (sister, which she stressed is ALWAYS with Damma - 'I will never say' otherwise), plus their possessives akhii/akhuuka and ukhtii/ukhtuka/ukhtuki, and the third book word ithbaat (proof, kasra under the alif). Her point about unvowelled text is the practical one: on street signs, in newspapers, even in books you will not see the Damma on ukht, and you must read it in anyway because you know the word. Then listening exercise 3 on page 68, six items read round the room - ibHaar (sailing), ithbaat, and the pair iKhbaar / aKhbaar that carried the real lesson (below), plus three items the transcription loses. She finished with drill 2, six words dictated and written AT THE BOARD by students (Weston, Nazra - who identified hers correctly as 'alif hamza and baa' - Clara and others), during which she gave her tashkiil policy: 'Again, I'm not so particular about the [tashkiil]. If it helps, put it. I need you at one point to start reading without the [tashkiil] completely like in Arab[ic]. But if it helps you, put it'

SPEAKING REVIEW, round-the-room, roughly 6 minutes and the reason she called today a speaking class - maa haadhaa ('what is this?') asked of picture after picture, with students called by name and a FULL SENTENCE demanded every time. Her reason for insisting on the full sentence rather than the bare noun: 'it helps you review all the words.' What actually got produced: haadhaa baab (this is a door); the hijab item, where a student asked whether you say Hijaabuka or Hijaabuki to a woman and she confirmed BOTH work in the sense that both are real forms, the -ki being the feminine addressee; baytuka; a negated nominal sentence, laa haadhaa laysa baytii ('no, this is not my house'), which she stopped to unpack because the student had built it correctly - negator, then the demonstrative, then laysa, then the noun - and she noted separately that laa is Arabic and lo is HEBREW, a correction she has now made more than once; haadhaa alif, where a student volunteered 'alif hamza' instead and she rated that MORE accurate; words containing baa' (baab, baaba, baytii); haadhaa raqam sab'a (this is number seven), where she made the student use raqam rather than name the digit bare, which is the number vocabulary from 9/22 being cashed in; and a 'what is she doing?' item answered with waajib (homework). She also probed what they have and have not been given for 'woman' - they have sitt, which she reminded them is specifically an OLDER lady and therefore wrong for the young woman in the picture, and mar'a has not been drilled

AN ARABIC WORSHIP SONG, about 6 minutes, played with a listening task attached ('try to find a word that you could identify') - students pulled out fii and one other word. Two things she taught off the back of it. First, a TRANSLATION point that is really a lesson about idiom: the English lyric 'you are my hiding place' becomes 'you are my ROCK' in the Arabic version, and her reading is that the Arabic came second, borrowed the English tune, and traded the literal image for one that would scan and rhyme - the same principle she applied later to the translation exercise. Second, a piece of cultural context she delivered flatly and without editorialising: the group is based in Israel and its English-language channel carries a name that its Arabic-language channel cannot, because 'anti-Semitism in the Arabic world is very high. So if you say anything in favor for Israel, you're cut right away from the culture.' The group's name is garbled in the transcript and I am not confident enough in it to record it. She recommended the songs as bilingual practice - 'you could sing in English and Arabic at the same time'

announcements.text: THE WRITING QUIZ CAME BACK, IT WAS SCORED OUT OF 20 NOT 10, AND A RETAKE IS ON OFFER BELOW HALF - this is the one thing in this lecture worth acting on. She handed the papers back, said 'many of you did really well, but those who didn't do well, please look at my corrections,' took them back in at the end ('I need these quizzes back... pass it, please'), and admitted a scale mix-up: she marked in her head out of 10, but the quiz is worth up to 20, so a paper mark of 5 is a 10 in Canvas. The retake rule as she stated it: below 5 on the paper, equivalently below 10 in Canvas, and you may retake to improve the grade - but the move is yours to make. 'You have to e-mail me, check my office hours, and tell me, can I come at this time to retake my quiz.' NO DEADLINE WAS GIVEN, which is why this is not in the commitments list, and is also why it can quietly expire - the action is to look up the Canvas score and, if it is under 10, email her with a specific office-hours time proposed.

GLOBAL FOCUS WEEK, TUESDAY 2026-09-29: TWO IDENTICAL SESSIONS ON ARABIC AND ISLAMIC CULTURE, 4:30 OR 6:30, AND HER HUSBAND IS THE SPEAKER. She called it 'an important commercial' and 'highly recommend[ed]' going. Registration is not optional plumbing: 'in order to go, you have to scan the QR code... They need to take head counts for how many people are attending. They're ordering food... If they have a limited place also, they won't let you in unless you registered.' Ministries and organisations will be on the first floor of a building whose name the transcript loses, and the QR code itself was on screen and is not recoverable from audio, so the registration link has to come from elsewhere (Liberty's Global Focus Week page or Center for Global Engagement). She was unsure whether she would be there herself. Recorded as a logistics commitment so it lands on the day without pretending to be graded work.

SHE RESTATED THE TAUGHT-LETTERS RULE IN RESPONSE TO A DIRECT QUESTION, AND IT IS THE RULE THAT GOVERNS WHAT A CARD SHOULD EVEN ASK FOR. A student asked whether there will come a point where she says a word and they must write the whole thing in Arabic. Her answer: 'Only when you know the whole letters.' Asked to confirm - 'So only memorize the one we know all the letters for?' - she said: 'In Arabic, and if there is one or two letters that you do not know, transliteration is fine.' She demonstrated it in the same breath, writing SaaHiba on the board while saying outright that they do not have the Saad yet and she is only 'preparing you for it for the future.' So production is gated to the taught set, transliteration is an accepted answer where a letter is missing, and today's list is a mix of both.

A DICTATION IS COMING AND SHE SAID PLAINLY THAT PRONUNCIATION IS WHAT WILL DETERMINE WHETHER YOU SPELL IT RIGHT - the second time in three classes she has made this exact argument. On jaami'a: 'make sure it's a ['ayn], not a [hamza], it's a superscripted C, so jaami'a, OK, jaami'a, not jaami'a, that will help you with the dictation for later.' On 9/22 she made the identical case about the 'ayn in arba'a. No dictation is dated beyond the Homework 5 drill 2 already on the list, but the pattern is that the words she makes the class over-articulate are the words that turn up in a dictation, and this hour that was jaami'a, arba'a, and the akh/ukht vowel contrast.

THE TWO NEW LETTERS SHE PROMISED FOR TODAY DID NOT ARRIVE, SO THE TAUGHT-LETTER SET DID NOT MOVE THIS WEEK. On 9/22 she said 'Thursday... I'll introduce 2 letters, but I don't know if the homework covers two or four of them.' What she actually did was a second pass on hamza plus the vocabulary list. Saad, Taa' and the word-final taa' were all put on the board and all three were explicitly labelled as NOT yet taught ('you don't know the Saad yet, but I'm showing it to you'; 'this one occurs only at the end of the word, so we learn it soon'; 'once we learn the taa', we'll talk about it'). Marked INFERRED because this is an absence rather than something she said - she never announced a change of plan - but it is load-bearing for anything gated on the taught set, and it means the Homework 5 drills she warned contain untaught letters are still being submitted without those letters having been covered.

WHAT IS TESTABLE ON HAMZA RIGHT NOW IS RECOGNITION AND READING, NOT THE RULES - she drew the line herself, twice. 'Later I'll teach you why this one is coming on the line, why this one is coming on [the alif]. Okay, but we'll leave that later because it's so complicated. For now, what I need you to do, recognize it and learn how to read it, read it correctly. Later, when we get more into grammar, we will learn the whys and the hows.' The same deferral covers the taa' marbuuTa pronunciation rule ('that's for grammar... once we learn that, I'll teach you that grammar rule') and the feminine-possessive form Taalibatuhaa ('that's harder... don't worry about this one... let's use masculine words for now'). Useful as a scope limit: a card demanding WHY a hamza takes a given seat is ahead of the course.

commitments.title: Global Focus Week session on Arabic and Islamic culture, Dr. Khouri's husband speaking - TWO identical sittings, 4:30pm or 6:30pm, pick one. She highly recommended it. You must register by QR code in advance: they are counting heads to order food and may turn away anyone unregistered if the room is capped. The QR code was on screen only, so the link has to be found on Liberty's Global Focus Week page. Optional, not graded

off_slide: She overrode her own textbook on the word for 'friend', and the correction is the kind that only comes from a native speaker. The book gives SaaHib / SaaHibii, and she stopped to warn them off it: in Shami, SaaHibii means a BOYFRIEND or GIRLFRIEND - 'we're so close, we're talking with each other about marriage, maybe before becoming fiances' - so 'if you are in Jordan, Lebanon, or Syria' and a man uses it of a woman, 'people would think they are in a relation.' Her replacement, which she 'highly suggest[ed]': rafiiq / rafiiqii (m) and rafiiqatii (f) for a friend of the opposite sex. Man to man, SaaHibii is fine and carries no weight at all - 'could be a friend, could be a roommate... doesn't have to be like close friendship.' She still wants both pairs learned.

The ROOT SYSTEM, taught opportunistically off two items in listening exercise 3 and not a scheduled topic - the single most useful thing in the hamza block. Item 5 is iKhbaar (to tell the news) and they already know aKhbaar (news): same consonants, and the ONLY difference is the hamza's vowel and whether it sits above or below the alif. Her framing: 'In Arabic, we have a system. It's kind of complicated, but also help you learn vocab without like learning really or memorizing... you just change the position of the Hamza and you get a different word.' She ran the same move on item 1, ibHaar (sailing), whose root is baHr (sea) - 'if you know the root, you know this word is related to something related to that root.' This is the first time a root-and-pattern account of Arabic vocabulary has appeared in the course.

Her method for translating INTO English, stated as a procedure rather than a remark, and worth keeping because it is how she will want the homework dictations read back: 'At the beginning, translate every word and then make, put them all together, let them make sense in English. Even if you had to change the position of the words, that's totally fine because we want them to make sense in the target language.' She then modelled it word by word on kitaabii wa waajibii fii baytii - my book, and, my homework, in my house - before assembling the sentence. Related grammar she dropped in while doing it: Arabic uses NO copula in these sentences, so al-ustaadha Khouri hiya ustaadhatii is 'Professor Khouri IS my professor' with no verb present.

Parker asked the sukuun question and got a real answer. He read the mark as a shortened vowel; she rejected that framing: 'It's not shortened, it's more to me, it's more like a silence. There is no tashkiil on that one. There is no A, O, E. It's just the bare sound.' She generalised it to every letter - baa/buu/bii carry vowels, with a sukuun the letter is silent - and then, notably, left the door open: 'This is how we think about it in Arabic, but if I don't know, if you have something else, different rationale, I don't mind it.'

The taa' marbuuTa was taught by stealth, through the possessive, before the letter itself has been introduced. SaaHiba sounds like it ends in -a, but it is written with a taa', and the proof she used is what happens when you add a possessive: SaaHiba + -ii surfaces the consonant as SaaHibatii. Same mechanism on Taaliba / Taalibatuhaa, and on jaami'a, where the taa' is pronounced in a possessive construction ('jaami'at Liberty') and not in isolation ('jaami'a'). She asked them to sit with the WHY rather than the form - 'I need you also to start thinking, why did she say, why the T with the feminine' - and deferred the actual rule.

The gendered imperative is not an abstraction in her classroom: tafaDDal and tafaDDalii are what she literally says when she sends a student to the board, 'so when I tell the ladies go to the board and write, I would say tafaDDalii, but to the man's tafaDDal.' The plural tafaDDaluu got the same treatment with a scenario - a group waiting at a door. She listed the word's uses deliberately: inviting someone in, handing someone food or coffee, and yielding the floor to a question.

She opened, as she does every class, with prayer by name over what students had raised in the room beforehand - a classmate whose shipment (three items, 88 dollars) went to the wrong address, and another with a graded presentation in a different course the next class - asking for 'the flow of speech and the charisma' for the presentation. Attendance was taken immediately after. This is the standing shape of the first two minutes and not a one-off.

The recording ends mid-activity. The pair/trio speaking task (introduce yourself and your partner, where he is from) was still being set up and negotiated - she moved from pairs to groups of three on the fly - when the 63 minutes ran out, so whatever she said while closing the class is not captured.
terms: tafaDDal / tafaDDalii / tafaDDaluu (go ahead, come in, please take it - m / f / pl; Shami itfaDDal, itfaDDalii)
yalla (let's go, come on - she flagged it as not respectful, unlike tafaDDal)
SaaHib / SaaHibii / SaaHiba / SaaHibatii (friend - but boyfriend/girlfriend in Shami; see off_slide)
rafiiq / rafiiqii / rafiiqatii (friend - her recommended word for a friend of the opposite sex)
huwa / hiya (he / she; Shami huwwe / hiyye) - Arabic has no neutral pronoun
-uhu (his) and -uhaa (her), both taking a Damma on the noun's last letter: ismuhu, ismuhaa
akh / akhii / akhuuka (brother, my brother, your brother) - alif-hamza with fatHa
ukht / ukhtii / ukhtuka / ukhtuki (sister and possessives) - always with Damma, even unwritten
ithbaat (proof) - kasra written UNDER the alif
ibHaar (sailing), from the root baHr (sea)
akhbaar (news) vs ikhbaar (to tell the news) - one root, distinguished only by the hamza
Taalib / Taaliba (student m / f) - the 'harsh T', Taa' not taa'
ustaadh / ustaadha (teacher, professor, Mister - one word for all three); borrowed profesor / profesora
jaami'a (university); jaami'at Liberty in a possessive construction
Saff (class, as in a class you sit in)
waajib / waajibuka / waajibuhu / waajibuhaa (homework and possessives)
bayt / baytuhu / baytuhaa (house; Shami bayto / bayta)
amriikii / amriikiyya (American m / f)
duktuur (doctor)
laysa (the negator for a nominal sentence: laa haadhaa laysa baytii)
raqam (number) - reused from 9/22 in haadhaa raqam sab'a
hamza 'on the line' - her name for a bare word-final hamza, as in the letter name baa'
seat (her term for the letter a hamza must sit on: alif, waaw, or a dotless yaa')
sukuun - absence of a vowel, 'a silence', not a shortened vowel
taa' marbuuTa (not yet named as a letter; taught through SaaHibatii, Taalibatuhaa, jaami'at)

make sure it's a ['ayn], not a [hamza], it's a superscripted C, so jaami'a, OK, jaami'a, not jaami'a, that will help you with the dictation for later
For now, what I need you to do, recognize it and learn how to read it, read it correctly. Later, when we get more into grammar, we will learn the whys and the hows.

transcription_notes: Teams ASR, 5,347 words / 589 cues over 63 min, and it handles spoken Arabic very badly - essentially every Arabic word in this file is misheard as an English one. Transliterations above are my reconstructions from context plus the 9/22 record, NOT what the file says; representative examples so a later reader can audit them: maa haadhaa appears as 'Mahada' / 'Maha the' / 'Mahala', laa haadhaa laysa baytii as 'La Hadaleisa Beiti', waajibii as 'wasabi', jaami'a as 'Jamia' / 'Jamaica' / 'Al Jumana', Damma as 'thumbna' / 'Amanda', tashkiil as 'the skill' / 'tishkir', sukuun as 'sukum' / 'second' / 'school', ukhtii as 'of tea', ithbaat as 'it's bad', and rafiiqatii once as 'Stephanie'. Where I could not reconstruct with confidence I said so instead of guessing: (1) the name of the worship group and its Arabic channel; (2) the building hosting Global Focus Week; (3) three of the six items in listening exercise 3 on page 68, including item 4; (4) the mid-word/end-word hamza example she glossed as 'to stutter' - the transcript gives no recoverable form, so the word is unnamed; (5) her answer to the on-or-under question about tashkiil placement asked at the 9/22 quiz, which a student raised again in effect here and which still is not on tape. Two substantive ambiguities to flag rather than smooth over. FIRST, 'drill 2': she said 'we're gonna do drill too... We have six, so six words' and ran it at the board. It is NOT determinable from the recording whether this is the unit 4 homework's drill 2 - the dictation due on Canvas Friday 2026-09-25 per the 9/22 record - or a separate in-section drill. The six words worked were hamza words, consistent with the day's lesson rather than with unit 4, which points at a book drill in the hamza section; but she never said a unit number, so the safe reading is that the Canvas dictation is still outstanding and should still be submitted. No commitment was added or removed on the strength of this. SECOND, she placed listening exercise 3 on PAGE 68 today, while the 9/22 record has exercises 1 through 3 on page 67; this may be the same exercise running across the page break or a slip by one of us, and it is not worth resolving from audio. POSITION DELIBERATELY OMITTED: she named no unit at any point today. The in-class work sat in unit 3 (page 68, hamza) while the new vocabulary list's unit is unstated, and the field's contract forbids inferring a unit from drift. Omitting it leaves position-watch on the 9/22 reading of 'unit 4', which is still the furthest unit the class has touched and is therefore correct. Quote timestamps are the start of the caption block containing the line, not the line itself.
